newsitem.title: USA: NCR CEO says expects '97 earnings to top '96.
newsitem.headline: NCR CEO says expects '97 earnings to top '96.

text.p: After AT&T Corp's soon-to-be-spun off computer unit, NCR Corp, turned around three months ahead of plan, NCR chief executive officer Lars Nyberg said Thursday and he expects 1997 earnings to top 1996's.
But the Dayton-based unit still has "a big hill to climb" to grow profits, he said in a telephone interview.
In 1995 NCR lost $722 million on sales of $8.1 billion.
NCR said its $29 million third-quarter operating profit, versus a year-ago operating loss of $196 million, put it $3 million in the black for 1996's first nine months.

NCR results were included in AT&T's third quarter report. AT&T acquired NCR in 1991 and plans to spin it off by yearend. AT&T said the share distribution has been approved as tax free for the company and shareholders. Last month AT&T spun off another unit, Lucent Technologies.
Nyberg declined to make specific earnings projections for the fourth quarter or for 1997.
"We will, of course, expect to improve our earnings in '97 over '96," he said. "We are already, at nine months, at break-even operating income level. That was the ambition for the full year."
Nyberg said he is pleased with the speed of the turnaround and credited NCR's 38,900 employees and its "demanding but supportive customers." But it is only the first step, he said.
"It's fantastic we've been able to break even, but going forward, we have to create profits," he said. "It's all about growing the business now."
NCR said that excluding discontinued products, orders were up strongly for the quarter and year-to-date over a year ago, which Nyberg said is an indicator of potential future growth.
"We are absolutely convinced that we can, with (our focused strategy), grow the business," Nyberg said.

The Swedish-born Nyberg joined NCR in June 1995. He was recruited from Philips Electronics N.V. to head the faltering unit, which pulled out of the low-end personal computer market last year. Its focus now is on markets where it is a world leader, such as retailing and financial services, Nyberg said.

NCR, founded more than 100 years ago as National Cash Register, is the number one maker of automated teller machines (ATMs) and of price scanners used in supermarkets and mass merchandise stores, he said. It is the number two maker of retail checkout point-of-sale systems, Nyberg said.
Acknowledging that the retail checkout equipment business is growing more slowly than some others, Nyberg said he does not foresee saturation in either that market nor in ATMs.

NCR hopes to unveil some exciting new retail products, he said. In addition, ATM use in supermarkets, malls and other non-bank locations, and in emerging countries, continues to grow, he said. NCR last month introduced a "mini-ATM" for sites other than banks.
NCR's data "warehousing" business is "more or less exploding," Nyberg said, referring to systems that store data so it is accessible and can be readily interpreted and used.
